outcome: For k≥5, Leng, Sah and Sawhney proved r_k(N) ≪ N·exp(-(log log N)^{c_k}) for some c_k>0, the first improvement to the upper bound on r_k(N) for k≥5 since Gowers's 2001 bound; the exact growth rate remains unknown and the problem is still open.
summary: This bullet asks for the growth rate of r_k(N), the size of the largest subset of {1,...,N} with no k-term arithmetic progression — a quantity for which the exact asymptotic order is unknown for every k≥3, so by the special carve-out in §3.1 ('a bullet asking for ... the value of a constant/record'), any bound improvement on this quantity is itself a change to what the bullet's entry would say, not a mere restriction of the question. The decisive event in the window is Leng, Sah and Sawhney's arXiv:2402.17995 ('Improved Bounds for Szemerédi's Theorem'), first posted 2024-02-28 (v2 2024-02-29), proving that for all k≥5 there is c_k>0 with r_k(N) ≪ N·exp(-(log log N)^{c_k}). This is the first improvement to the k≥5 upper bound since Gowers's 2001 result r_k(N) < N/(log log N)^{c_k}, and it was digested by experts: Quanta Magazine's 2024-08-05 feature quotes Ben Green (Oxford) calling it 'phenomenally impressive' and the authors' advisor Yufei Zhao calling it 'a huge achievement.' I classify this as `resolved`-adjacent but coded `progress` rather than `resolved` or `partial`, because the problem itself (determine the true growth rate) remains open — only the known bound moved; no case of the full problem was settled and no journal acceptance was found (as of this search the paper is still an arXiv preprint, not yet listed as journal-published). I found no involvement of any AI system in this work: the paper's own text (as much as could be extracted), the Quanta article, and general search turned up nothing about AI/ML/LLM assistance — this appears to be entirely human mathematical work built on companion paper arXiv:2402.17994 (quasipolynomial Gowers inverse theorem bounds) and prior work of Green, Tao and Ziegler. Separately, for k=3, Bloom and Sisask's r_3(N) bound (arXiv:2302.07211, originally 2023, revised to v3 in 2025-05) predates the window for its core result and is not treated as a fresh event; I found one small 2026 arXiv computational note (2606.04016, solo author Mehmet Ergezer) reporting a SAT/ILP/Lean computational search supporting the specific value r_3(212)=43, but this is a single finite-N computational data point, not a growth-rate bound, and its abstract discloses no AI involvement either — I judged it out of scope for this bullet (it doesn't move an asymptotic growth-rate bound) and did not use it as the basis for status or dating.
competing_reading: One could argue this bullet, being an open-ended 'determine the growth rate' request rather than a bullet explicitly asking for a record/constant value, should be treated like an ordinary existence/infinitude question where narrowing an unknown quantity doesn't count as a change (per the general rule in §3.1) — under that stricter reading the correct status would be `open` with `no_change_found` true, since no one has determined the actual growth rate, only moved a bound. I judged the growth-rate/bound exception in §3.1 ('a bullet asking for a largest known object or the value of a constant') to apply here because r_k(N)'s asymptotic order is precisely a 'value of a function/constant' the bullet asks to pin down, and bound movements are the only kind of progress that can ever occur on such a bullet before full resolution.
what_would_settle_it: A published statement (or triage-level consensus) clarifying whether 'determine growth rate of X' bullets are to be scored like record/constant bullets (any bound movement counts) or like existence/infinitude bullets (only full resolution counts) would remove this ambiguity.
